claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid physics-informed framework will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness more accurately and efficiently than current high-fidelity methods.
The proposed framework couples machine-learning predictions with low-fidelity mesoscale simulations.
CALPHAD-informed phase behavior will be incorporated into the mesoscale simulations.
A small set of tensile and fracture measurements will be sufficient for experimental calibration.
The framework requires a sufficiently comprehensive simulation-generated and experimental training dataset.
The framework is intended to operate under standard laboratory tensile and fracture-testing conditions.
Reliability requires retention of the reported hierarchical heterostructure without significant post-manufacturing alteration.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations mediate Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The multilevel chemical fluctuations will be explicitly represented in simulation variables and machine-learning descriptors.
Mesoscale simulations can capture phase and microstructural evolution under applied stress.
Machine learning can rapidly interpolate mesoscale results using validated experimental data.
Physics-based constraints will reduce computational demand and improve accuracy relative to pure ab initio or CALPHAD methods.
The hybrid model will improve prediction accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness by 15–20%.
The hybrid model will reduce computational time by approximately tenfold relative to conventional ab initio or CALPHAD-only approaches.
Conventional trial-and-error exploration of the large HEA composition space is impractical.
CALPHAD and machine-learning approaches have been proposed for efficient HEA composition, phase, or mechanical-property prediction.
Existing ab initio, CALPHAD, and stand-alone machine-learning methods have limited predictive capability, especially for fracture toughness.
Significant thermal or mechanical alteration of the hierarchical microstructure will make the framework unreliable.
Training data that omit relevant compositional or microstructural variations will cause extrapolation errors and loss of reliability.
